instruction: I cried when my mom had to go and now I can't stop. When will she be back?
response: Crying when someone you love leaves is completely normal, and it shows how much you care about your mom. She didn't go far — she might be in the waiting room, getting a coffee, or taking a quick rest, because taking care of you takes a lot of energy for grown-ups too. Your nurse knows how to reach her if you need her right away. You can also press the call button on your bed and ask. She'll be back as soon as she can, and until then, every single person in this building is here to help keep you safe.

instruction: I don't want any more needles. I already had two and that's enough.
response: Two needles is a lot, and it makes total sense that you don't want any more. Your care team knows exactly how you're feeling — you're allowed to tell them that too. Here at Children's Hospital there's something called the Comfort Promise, which means your team will do everything they can to make things hurt less. That includes numbing cream on your skin before anything goes in, so you barely feel the poke. You can also ask your nurse how many more needle things are planned, so you're not surprised. You're being so brave, and your feelings about it matter.

instruction: Everything smells different here and it makes me feel yucky.
response: You're right, hospitals do smell different from home — it's mostly the cleaning products they use to keep everything really safe and germ-free for all the kids here. That smell can feel a bit overwhelming, especially if you're already not feeling great. If it bothers you a lot, you can ask a nurse to open a window if possible, or bring something from home that smells nice — like a favourite lotion, a stuffed animal, or even a piece of clothing that smells like home. Some kids find that helps a lot.

instruction: What if I get scared in the night and nobody comes?
response: Someone will always come — that's a promise. There are nurses here all night long, every single night. They don't go home like other people do. Right next to your bed there's a call button, and the moment you press it, a nurse gets notified and comes to check on you. You don't have to be in a big emergency to press it — if you're scared, that's a completely good reason. Some kids keep the call button in their hand when they're trying to sleep, just so they know it's right there. You will never be left alone.

instruction: I heard the doctor talking outside my room and they said something about my blood. Is something really bad happening to me?
response: It can be really scary to hear grown-ups talking about you when you don't have all the words to understand what they mean. But here's the thing — doctors talk about blood tests all the time, because blood is like a little message from your body that tells them how you're doing. It doesn't mean something really bad is happening. It usually means they're checking. The best thing to do is ask your doctor or nurse directly: 'Can you explain what you were saying?' You always have the right to know what's going on with your own body, in words that make sense to you. Your parents can help ask too.

instruction: I want to go home right now. Can you make them let me go home?
response: Wanting to go home is one of the most normal feelings in the world when you're in the hospital, and it's okay to really, really want that. The reason you're staying is because your doctors want to make sure you're safe and feeling better before you leave — not to keep you here for no reason. I can't make that decision, but your doctor can explain exactly what needs to happen before you can go home. Sometimes knowing the plan makes the waiting easier. You can ask your nurse: 'What does my body need to do before I can go home?' That way you have something to look forward to.

instruction: My tummy hurts from being scared, not from being sick. What do I do?
response: Your body is really smart — when you're scared or worried, it actually does make your tummy hurt, because your feelings and your body are connected like that. That kind of tummy hurt is real, even if it's not from being sick. There are a few things that might help: taking some slow deep breaths in through your nose and out through your mouth, asking a nurse for a warm blanket for your belly, or telling your mom or dad how you're feeling so they can sit with you. The Child Life team here at Children's Hospital also helps kids with scary feelings — your nurse can connect you with them.

instruction: I don't want to take a bath here. I only like baths at home.
response: That makes a lot of sense — baths at home feel safe and familiar, and here everything is different. You don't have to have a bath if it doesn't feel right today. You can always do a gentle wash with a warm cloth instead, which lots of kids prefer in the hospital anyway. If there's a specific thing that makes bath time at home feel better — a special soap, a toy you keep in the tub, a certain way things are done — you can tell your nurse and they'll try their best to make it feel more like home. Your comfort matters here.

instruction: The other kid in the next room was crying really loud. Will that happen to me too?
response: It can be hard to hear other kids who are upset — your feelings about that are completely understandable. Every kid at Children's Hospital is here for different reasons, and what's happening for them isn't the same as what's happening for you. Your care team knows your specific situation and they'll always tell you what to expect before anything happens. You'll never be surprised without warning. And if you're ever feeling scared or upset yourself, it's completely okay to show it — crying is one of the ways our bodies let out big feelings, and nobody here will think less of you for it.

instruction: I keep having bad dreams since I got here. What do I do?
response: Bad dreams can happen when our brain is trying to work through something stressful, and being in the hospital is definitely stressful. There are some things that can help: keeping something familiar nearby like a stuffed animal or a blanket from home, having a parent or trusted adult nearby when you fall asleep, and telling your nurse if the bad dreams are really bothering you — they can check if anything, like a medicine or the room lighting, might be making sleep harder. Some kids also find it helps to tell someone about the dream so it feels less powerful. You're safe here, and your team wants you to feel that way even while you sleep.

instruction: I've been putting on a brave face for my parents but honestly I'm terrified and I don't know how to tell them.
response: That takes a lot of strength to recognize — and a lot of energy to keep up. You don't have to protect your parents from knowing you're scared. Most of the time, they already sense it, and giving them the chance to actually be there for you can help both of you. You don't have to have the perfect words. Something like 'I'm more scared than I've been letting on' is enough to open the door. If talking directly to them feels too hard, a nurse, a social worker, or one of the Child Life specialists here can help you find the words or even be in the room when you have that conversation. You're allowed to need support too.

instruction: I feel like everyone knows what's going on with me except me. Nobody explains anything directly.
response: That's a legitimate frustration, and you're right to name it. You are the patient — you have every right to understand what's happening with your own body, in clear language, not just fragments between people who assume someone else explained it. A good starting point is being direct with your doctor or nurse: 'I need you to walk me through my situation from the beginning, like I'm hearing it for the first time.' You can also ask them to slow down or repeat things. If you find it's still not happening, Patient Relations at Children's Hospital LHSC can help ensure your communication needs are being met. You don't have to accept being kept in the dark.

instruction: I hate that I have to ask permission for everything. I'm not a little kid.
response: That feeling of lost autonomy is one of the hardest parts of being hospitalized as a teenager — and it's completely valid. You're at an age where independence matters, and a lot of hospital routines don't account for that. Where you do have choices, take them: what you wear, when you sleep if it's flexible, who's in the room during examinations. For the things that feel like they require permission, it's worth asking your care team which decisions are actually yours to make. In Ontario, older teens have a growing set of rights around medical decisions. Knowing where you do have agency can make the things you can't control feel a bit more manageable.

instruction: My friends are posting stuff online and I'm stuck here missing everything. I feel like my whole life is passing me by.
response: That feeling is real and it's hard — watching everyone else continue normally while your world has been put on pause. FOMO is difficult enough outside the hospital; inside it can feel especially isolating. A few things that help some people: staying connected in smaller ways (a text, a voice note, even just reacting to things) without the pressure of explaining everything; letting one trusted friend be your link to that world rather than trying to keep up with everything; and being honest with yourself that you're not missing your life — you're dealing with something important that takes priority right now, even when that's unfair. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre on B1 also has resources to help with keeping up with school and social connection.

instruction: I keep thinking about what happens if the treatment doesn't work. Is it okay to think about that?
response: Yes — it's completely okay, and honestly it would be more unusual not to. When you're in a situation like this, your mind naturally goes to the worst-case scenarios as a way of trying to prepare. Thinking about it doesn't make it more likely to happen. What matters is what you do with those thoughts — whether they're something you're carrying alone or something you can say out loud to someone you trust. Your care team includes people whose specific job is to support you emotionally through exactly this kind of fear. You don't have to pretend you're only thinking about the positive outcomes. Being honest about the scary thoughts is often what makes them a little less consuming.

instruction: I'm embarrassed about some of the things the doctors have to do to me. Is that normal?
response: Very much so — feeling embarrassed or self-conscious about examinations and procedures is one of the most common things teenagers experience in hospital, and your care team has seen it a thousand times without judgment. You're allowed to ask for privacy during any examination: to have the door fully closed, to have only the people who absolutely need to be there in the room, and to have non-essential people step out. If having a doctor of a specific gender makes you more comfortable, you can request that too. Your comfort and dignity are taken seriously here, and there's nothing wrong with advocating for what you need.

instruction: I don't want to talk to the counselor. I just want someone to actually listen to me without writing stuff down.
response: That's a really clear thing to know about yourself, and it's worth telling someone. You can say exactly that to a nurse or a Child Life specialist: 'I don't want to be assessed or documented right now — I just need someone to listen.' Child Life specialists in particular are trained for exactly that kind of presence, and their conversations aren't part of your formal medical record. You can also be honest with any counselor who comes to see you: if you're not ready or not in the right headspace, saying 'I'm not up for this today' is completely within your rights.

instruction: I feel guilty that my family is spending so much money because of me being here.
response: That kind of guilt says a lot about how much you care about your family — but it's putting weight on you that shouldn't be yours to carry. Your being here isn't a choice you made, and your health is not a burden they resent. If financial stress is real for your family, there are social workers at Children's Hospital who can help connect your family to financial assistance programs, social supports, and resources specifically for families in this situation. It might help to talk to a social worker directly — not to fix it yourself, but to know that systems exist for this so your family doesn't have to navigate it alone.

instruction: I've been here so long I don't even know what day it is anymore.
response: Losing track of time is genuinely disorienting, and it happens to a lot of people in hospital — the routines blur, every day looks the same, and the outside world starts to feel distant. A few small things can help re-anchor you: keeping your phone's date visible, asking a nurse or family member to recap what day it is when they come in, or even keeping a simple note in your phone about what's happening each day. It also helps to have something to look forward to, even small — a visit, a show, a specific meal. If you're finding that the time loss is connected to your mood feeling very low or flat, that's worth mentioning to your care team.

instruction: My roommate keeps having visitors and I haven't had any in three days.
response: Three days without visitors is genuinely hard, especially when you can see other people getting that support right next to you. It's okay to feel lonely about that — that's a human response, not a complaint. A few options: if there are people who want to visit but haven't organized it, a nurse can help coordinate visiting logistics. If family or friends are far away, video calls are a real alternative and your nurse can help you find a private space for that. The Child Life team can also spend time with you during visits if you want company that isn't about your medical situation. You don't have to just wait it out.
